Report ID: LV-20261126-1412
Status: Final project submission
Project scope: Cross-hospital sepsis prediction, reproducible experimentation, and automated AWS delivery
Revision: 5 - Expanded Step Functions workflow and ECS task mapping

Executive summary

The implemented research pipeline successfully processed the complete public PhysioNet Challenge 2019 training cohorts, trained and compared four classical models, reproduced the supplied experiment’s aggregate results, and served the selected model through a local scoring API.

The solution was also deployed and tested on AWS using GitHub Actions, ECS Fargate, and AWS Lambda. Its infrastructure-as-code supports containerized training, experiment tracking, approval-based model publication, authenticated serverless scoring, and operational monitoring.

The project demonstrates end-to-end software execution, numerical reproducibility, and cloud delivery. These engineering outcomes are distinct from clinical validation or a new independent external validation study.

Project objective Outcome
Does the complete local software test suite pass? Yes: 145 tests passed; none skipped. Warnings remain.
Can the pipeline process the complete available real dataset? Yes: 40,336 stays and 1,552,210 hourly rows passed hard schema checks.
Are the supplied model results reproducible? Yes: validation and held-out aggregate metrics matched within the recorded numeric tolerances.
Does local inference agree with batch/CLI inference? Yes: the recorded 51-hour parity case had zero probability difference and identical decisions and notifications.
Does the local container work? Yes: build and synthetic end-to-end smoke checks passed on Linux ARM64.
Does the model transport without degradation? No: Hospital B discrimination, utility, and early-detection recall were lower, with monitoring alerts.
Was the solution deployed and tested on AWS? Yes: GitHub Actions delivery, Fargate compute, and Lambda scoring. The AWS architecture and release stages are described below.
How are model releases controlled? Step Functions orchestrates training, an approval pause, frozen evaluation, and publication; scoring loads a checksum-pinned model.
Is clinical use supported by this evidence? No.

Histogram gradient boosting was selected at a 0.06 probability threshold, with a six-hour notification cooldown and an empirical validation budget of 0.20 false alert events per nonseptic patient-day. External Hospital B results were AUROC 0.7635, average precision 0.0620, normalized hourly utility 0.2340, early-detection recall 0.4393, and false-alert burden 0.1294 per nonseptic patient-day.

The operating budget was met in the observed cohorts, but this did not prevent loss of detection performance. The demonstrated system remains a research application, not a clinical decision-making tool.

Project scope and experimental design

What was executed

The recorded run covered:

  • The complete unit/invariant test suite, causal-feature script, and synthetic demo.
  • Real-data preparation, saved splits, hard schema validation, and diagnostic extreme-value counts.
  • SIRS and always-no baselines; four candidate models; calibration, selection, and held-out evaluation.
  • Supplementary missingness, SIRS failure-pattern, and hospital-comparison analyses.
  • Local MLflow tracking, saved-model replay, API parity/validation, and nine latency scenarios.
  • Monitoring-reference construction and both internal- and external-test monitoring replays.
  • Docker build and synthetic container serving checks.
  • Browser inspection of the MLflow run, API documentation, and interactive synthetic ward replay.
  • Hospital B API examples and synthetic robustness probes for split and feature contracts.

Measurement scope

The detailed test counts, model metrics, and latency measurements in this report belong to the recorded full-cohort research run. The AWS section describes the extended deployment implementation and its environment parameters. Cloud deployment does not turn local latency measurements into cloud performance measurements. Hosted run IDs, cloud latency distributions, and release-specific rollback results are not included in the experiment record. DVC push/reproduction, notebook execution, and separate experimental HMM fitting are outside the recorded run.

Full-cohort training used the native Python environment. The container smoke test trained and served a synthetic model inside the image; it did not certify full-cohort container training or real-model cross-platform operation.

The dataset was already present locally; no fresh download was required. Existing datasets and experiment outputs were preserved. Runtime source code was not changed to obtain these results.

The original repository snapshot had no available Git commit, so this is not a commit-addressed release certification. An additional report-time digest of the experimental source/configuration files is recorded in the evidence manifest; it does not retroactively restore the missing training revision.

AWS design and deployment

Infrastructure and environment configuration

The platform is defined by the extended CloudFormation root stack, its nested templates, and the deployment automation. The infrastructure separates artifact storage, training orchestration, experiment tracking, serving, and observability.

The development configuration selects ECS Fargate training, MLflow on ECS with RDS PostgreSQL, and Evidently monitoring. SageMaker is disabled in this profile. Scoring defaults to Lambda. This is different from the root template’s generic SageMaker defaults; the diagrams show the development profile rather than combining mutually exclusive backends.

Fargate training uses a dedicated VPC with two public subnets and controlled task security groups, avoiding a NAT gateway. Public task IP assignment does not make the MLflow database public: RDS has PubliclyAccessible=false. The optional Fargate scoring mode uses a separate network design with an internal ALB and private tasks. These two Fargate use cases are not the same deployment topology.

Architecture overview

The first view connects automated delivery to the governed model lifecycle. GitHub OIDC supplies temporary deployment credentials; CloudFormation assembles the platform; ECR stores separate training, scoring, Lambda, and tools images. Step Functions runs prepare, tune, and train tasks, pauses for approval through SNS, then evaluates and publishes the frozen model.

Editable deployment diagram (SVG).

The expanded workflow maps each ecs:runTask.sync state to its own ECS task invocation. All four invocations reuse the revision created by RegisterTaskDefinition; their mode and capacity-provider overrides select the work. Train uses the entry point’s default train mode. CheckPrepare can bypass preparation. Approval and notification states use SNS, not ECS; the four exit-code checks and the summarized failure route are shown separately from the normal execution path.

Editable Step Functions/ECS workflow (SVG).

The runtime view shows the Lambda scoring and telemetry path. Signed requests reach the live alias through an IAM-authenticated function URL. The function loads a SHA-256-pinned bundle from S3 and uses DynamoDB as an alert-delivery ledger. CloudWatch prediction records flow through Firehose to S3.

Editable application/operations diagram (SVG). Solid connectors show the principal request, artifact, or telemetry flows. Dashed connectors identify configuration-dependent monitoring and release controls, not components that are always enabled.

The diagrams use the official July 2026 AWS Architecture Icons. The figures are derived from template resources, conditions, and deployment commands; they are architecture views, not account-specific resource inventories.

Component responsibilities and implementation

Component Responsibility Implementation

Step Functions and Fargate Govern training and publication. Prepare, tune, train, approval callback, evaluate/publish, and failure notifications.
MLflow, RDS, and S3 Experiment tracking and model registry. ECS-hosted MLflow, non-public PostgreSQL metadata, S3 artifacts, candidate/production aliases.

Lambda Authenticated scoring. Function URL with AWS IAM, live alias, pinned model URI/hash, DynamoDB ledger.
S3 and KMS Artifact and telemetry retention. Encrypted/versioned artifacts, model publications, prediction logs, and lifecycle policies.
CloudWatch, Firehose, and SNS Runtime telemetry and notifications. Prediction-log subscription to Firehose/S3, infrastructure alarms, approval and failure messages.

Evidently on ECS Drift reports and UI. Enabled in the development profile; separate report task, UI service, and drift alarm.

Release controls, alternatives, and operational learnings

The deployment stages are validate, plan, stack/images, readiness, optional retraining, publish/serve, smoke test, verify, and record state. The deployment helper passes the published ModelS3Uri and ModelSha256 into the serving stack. Both the Lambda entry point and the Fargate serving command support checksum-verified model retrieval; the earlier local-only image path is not the cloud model-delivery mechanism.

The Lambda template uses versioned aliases and configurable CodeDeploy traffic shifting with error/duration alarms. The development profile deliberately selects AllAtOnce; the root template also supports canary and linear policies. Human approval remains in the training/publication lifecycle regardless of whether a drift alarm starts a new candidate run.

Optional modes are explicit:

  • TrainingBackend=sagemaker replaces ECS training tasks with SageMaker jobs.
  • MlflowBackend=sagemaker enables the SageMaker MLflow App instead of ECS/RDS.
  • ServingMode=fargate replaces Lambda scoring with ALB/private Fargate serving.
  • A private API Gateway/WAF stack requires PrivateApiVpcEndpointId; it is not part of the baseline Lambda function-URL path.
  • Scheduled drift requires DriftReferenceS3Uri; an alarm-to-training rule additionally requires the pipeline and RetrainImageTag. Neither implies automatic production promotion.

The main operational learning is to separate deployment health from model validity. Infrastructure alarms, checksum checks, and successful requests do not establish calibration, retained cross-hospital sensitivity, or acceptable clinical risk.

Cost and reliability trade-offs

The ECS backend provides a training route when SageMaker access or instance quotas are constrained. Pipeline tasks run on demand, with Spot capacity for tuning/training. Lambda scoring can scale to zero, but ECS-hosted MLflow, Evidently, and RDS are not a zero-standing-cost platform; the power controls start and stop hosted tools. The development budget is USD 20 per month as an alert threshold, not a spending cap.

The development RDS configuration is single-AZ with a one-day backup retention period. It suits a demonstration rather than a high-availability clinical service. Production extensions include stronger recovery targets, tighter deployment-role permissions after bootstrap, and explicit availability and cost measurements.

Dataset, method, and operating policy

Complete-cohort selection and split verification

Preflight found that the unused local directory named physionet-full contained 20,335 Hospital A records. The complete local copy, physionet-complete-20261114, contained the expected 20,336 A records and 20,000 B records and was used instead. Directory names were not treated as evidence of completeness.

Split Source ICU stays Septic stays Hourly rows
Training A 11,183 984 435,449
Calibration A 3,051 269 117,195
Validation A 3,051 268 118,668
Internal test A 3,051 269 118,903
External test B 20,000 1,142 761,995
Total A and B 40,336 2,932 1,552,210

Splitting used seed 42, stratified source-A stays, and whole-record assignment rather than patient-hour splitting. The saved assignment and the actual training manifest were checked for one-to-one agreement. Actual input and split-file SHA-256 values were checked against the recorded metadata.

The unit is an ICU stay, not a known person. The dataset does not provide person identifiers sufficient to guarantee person-disjoint evaluation.

Hospital B was excluded from estimator fitting, calibration, and model/threshold selection in this execution. However, B has been inspected in earlier exploration and repeated evaluations. It is an exploratory external cohort, not a newly untouched, blinded confirmatory holdout.

Data validation and feature construction

All 40,336 stays and 1,552,210 rows passed the implemented hard rules: required columns, numeric measurements, no infinite values, valid nondecreasing binary labels, and consecutive recorded ICU hours.

Passing these checks does not prove that every value is physiologically plausible. Extreme-value diagnostic flags were retained for investigation rather than automatically clipped or silently discarded.

The selected pipeline used 276 features, a six-hour feature window, patient-local forward filling, missingness/never-observed indicators, measurement age, and trailing summaries. Learned imputation/scaling and estimators were fitted on training data; sigmoid calibration used a separate calibration cohort. Constant-prior predictions were not separately calibrated. Administrative unit codes and record/hospital identifiers were excluded from model inputs.

Selection policy and metric interpretation

Models and probability thresholds were selected using A validation only. Threshold candidates were evaluated against the empirical notification budget; the candidate model with the highest normalized hourly utility was selected, with the implemented false-alert/AP tie-breaks.

The following distinctions apply throughout this report:

  • Target: SepsisLabel is the supplied benchmark label, already shifted six hours before dataset-defined onset. It is not shifted again.
  • Probability: the score estimates that benchmark label, not a clinically validated probability of first sepsis onset within the next six hours.
  • Hourly decision versus notification: hourly_positive applies the threshold every hour; alert_event additionally enforces the cooldown.
  • Utility: normalized hourly utility uses hourly decisions and the published challenge weighting, not cooldown-suppressed notifications.
  • False-alert budget: events in stays that never have a positive label, divided by their observed hours/24. It does not count every potentially unhelpful notification in an eventual septic stay.
  • Early-detection recall: useful pre-onset notifications divided by eligible septic stays. First-row-positive stays and records ending before inferred onset are excluded. This is not hourly label recall.
  • Lead time: retrospective and inferred. It is not prospective proof of additional treatment time or clinical benefit.

No new threshold or model setting was selected from B results during this verification. The validation budget is a demonstration policy, not a clinician-approved tolerance.

Warnings and execution exceptions

The passing test run emitted a Starlette/httpx deprecation warning, empty-histogram NumPy warnings, and one test-fixture logistic-regression convergence warning at its 500-iteration limit. The recorded full-cohort training log did not contain that convergence warning. Warnings were not treated as proof of model failure, nor were they suppressed or reported as an error-free run.

An optional MLflow assistant-configuration endpoint initially returned HTTP 500 during first browser load; a retry returned HTTP 200. The main run page, finished status, and metrics rendered successfully. This was an ancillary UI initialization issue, not a failed training or tracking run.

Relative to A internal test, B AUROC was 0.0631 lower, utility was 0.1325 lower, and early-detection recall was 10.36 percentage points lower. These are descriptive differences; no confidence intervals or significance claim are supplied.

B has a lower positive-hour prevalence. Consequently, its lower AP and Brier score cannot be interpreted as pure changes in ranking and calibration, respectively. In particular, the lower Brier score on B is not sufficient evidence of improved calibration.

The model reduced false-alert burden by 91.5% relative to the standard SIRS comparator, but early-detection recall was lower. SIRS exceeded the 0.20 budget by approximately 7.59 times. It is therefore inaccurate to describe the model as better on every dimension.

Outcome: constrained notification behavior and positive benchmark utility were demonstrated. Acceptable clinical sensitivity, calibrated individual risk, and benefit to patients were not established.

Monitoring, shift, and subgroup learnings

Frozen reference and windowing

The reference used A-training inputs and A-validation scores/performance from the frozen bundle. The replay checked the bundle SHA-256 against that reference. Default fast windows target 2,000 patient-hours; slow windows target 20,000 patient-hours, with whole stays kept together.

These are seeded, shuffled retrospective windows, not observed calendar-time monitoring periods. Minimum sample rules remain active. Tail records that cannot fill a window are reported but not assessed as a monitoring window. The pooled cohort metrics still use the full scored cohort.

The performance reference uses the same validation cohort that selected the threshold, so some optimism is expected. Many statistics are checked in each window; isolated warnings are not independent statistical discoveries. Fast alerts generally require consecutive breaches, while schema failures are immediate.

Observed monitoring statuses

Check A internal alerts/windows B external alerts/windows B insufficient windows
Schema 0/58 0/376 0
Missingness 0/58 375/376 0
Input drift 0/58 313/376 0
Score drift 0/58 139/376 0
Alert rate 0/58 20/376 0
Calibration 0/5 0/38 1
Discrimination 0/5 26/38 1
Utility 1/5 23/38 1
Early detection 0/5 9/38 1
False-alert burden 0/5 0/38 1
Subgroup gap 0/5 0/38 8

An additional new-variable check warned in all 376 B fast windows and never escalated to an alert, by design. Check families overlap; counts must not be added to infer a number of independent incidents. Denominators above include insufficient windows, which are not passing windows.

Interpretation

  • Schema validity is not distribution stability. B passed schema checks while missingness, inputs, and scores shifted substantially.
  • Lower notification burden is not proof of retained sensitivity. B stayed within budget while discrimination, utility, and early recall degraded.
  • Fast drift alone is not model failure. Here, slow settled-label checks also supplied evidence of performance degradation.
  • The internal cohort was not uniformly quiet. One of its five slow windows raised a utility alert. This requires review of variability and case mix, not automatic dismissal or post-hoc relaxation of thresholds.
  • No calibration alert does not mean every calibration check passed. B had 32 OK, five warning, and one insufficient calibration window.
  • No automatic retraining occurred. A model, calibration, or policy change requires approval, a new bundle/reference, and suitable new evaluation data.

B tails not assessed as windows were 1,002 fast-window hours and 1,114 slow-window hours. A internal tails were 1,432 and 18,782 hours, respectively. The latter is material relative to the five evaluated internal slow windows and should temper conclusions about monitoring coverage.

Missingness and subgroup outcomes

The training/validation missingness study completed on 11,183 training and 3,051 validation stays. Across five fixed logistic-regression strategies, validation AP ranged from 0.0891 to 0.0985 and AUROC from 0.7133 to 0.7862. The highest AP and highest AUROC came from different strategies. These exploratory variants were not substituted into the selected model and are not an equivalent-feature comparison with the main pipeline.

The pooled external subgroup utility estimates were:

Recorded attribute Group Septic stays Normalized utility
Sex Female 495 0.2434

Age Under 45 200 0.2182
Age 45-64 427 0.2227

These descriptive estimates do not establish fairness. Eight external subgroup-monitoring windows lacked sufficient data; confidence intervals, broader attributes, and prespecified subgroup acceptance criteria are absent.

Serving and performance results

Request contract and functional examples

The API is stateless: every request supplies one stay’s history from its first available recorded ICU hour through the current hour. Omitted clinical fields mean missing observations. Labels, hospital IDs, administrative unit codes, and unknown measurement fields are rejected.

The native API loaded the newly trained real-data model with the expected bundle checksum. Recorded parity checks confirmed matching CLI/API probabilities, identical threshold decisions/notifications, and unchanged prefix results.

A separately selected Hospital B functional example had benchmark label 0 initially and label 1 by hour 6. Sending the complete six-row prefix, without the label, produced:

Final example hour Model probability Threshold Hourly positive Notification
6 0.07770351104741265 0.06 1 1

This case was deliberately selected to exercise the positive response path. It is not a random performance sample or independent evidence of clinical detection. A positive benchmark label is not a diagnosis of sepsis at that hour. No individual measurements or original record identifiers are included in this submission.

Local API latency

The benchmark used synthetic request histories against the native real-model API, with 50 measured requests and five warmups per scenario. Across nine scenarios there were 450 measured requests and zero failures. The separately recorded first request took 61.5 ms.

History hours Concurrent clients p50 ms p95 ms p99 ms Requests/s
24 1 14.9 26.4 30.4 61.14
24 4 60.7 88.6 108.2 61.68
24 8 124.8 195.9 229.1 61.49
72 1 13.5 16.0 61.8 69.20
72 4 61.5 89.9 123.3 61.92
72 8 128.3 178.2 210.0 64.34
336 1 13.7 15.0 34.9 70.29
336 4 61.4 83.4 101.7 63.03
336 8 141.1 219.5 254.9 54.76

The observed p95 range was 15.0-219.5 ms. Concurrency increased latency, consistent with serialized prediction under the service lock. These short, same-host measurements are not a sustained-load, soak, production-network, or availability test. With only 50 measured requests per row, p99 estimates should not be treated as stable tail-latency guarantees. No agreed latency SLO was available, so this is a measurement result, not an SLO pass. The host was shared rather than dedicated to this test. Memory high-water marks and total training wall time were not formally profiled.

Engineering challenges and improvements

Checksum-bound cloud model delivery

The extended Fargate service definition passes the model S3 URI and checksum explicitly. The shared cloud loader requires a pinned SHA-256 for S3 models; the Lambda entry point uses the same loading path and initializes the DynamoDB ledger. This closes the architectural gap between an image expecting a local model file and an independently published cloud model.

Research-pipeline robustness: hospital isolation

The saved-split loader validates split names and record membership but does not enforce the hospital/split boundary. An isolated synthetic probe reassigned 30 B stays to training and the loader accepted them.

Improvement: reject duplicate assignments, disallowed hospital/split combinations, and dataset/split identity mismatches before training; add a regression test for the rejected case.

Research-pipeline robustness: monitoring split identity

Monitoring setup regenerates cohorts from a seed instead of consuming a model-bound immutable assignment. A synthetic seed-7 model accepted a seed-42 reference: its monitoring validation cohort contained eight original training stays and six original internal-test stays.

Improvement: bind model, exact dataset, and saved split manifest; refuse mismatches at setup and replay.

Research-pipeline robustness: transformation semantics

The service compatibility check checks feature availability, and the recorded hash covers ordered column names rather than transformation behavior. A synthetic probe multiplied HR__last by ten without renaming columns. Startup remained ok, the hash was unchanged, and predictions changed.

Improvement: an enforced transformation-contract version or implementation digest, supported dependency compatibility, and saved-bundle prediction-parity regression tests.

Scope of the three robustness probes: these are deliberately adversarial synthetic probes. They do not show contamination in the correctly configured full-cohort run, whose actual saved/training assignments and hashes matched. Passing 145 existing tests did not detect these missing safeguards.

Reproducibility and release identity

The fresh run now includes verified split/source hashes, but still records git_commit: null. In addition, the training manifest path can substitute an ID hash for a data-content hash when Parquet inputs lack adjacent raw files. That fallback was not used for this raw-file training run.

Improvement: a release manifest linking a committed source revision, data/split content hashes, dependency lock, model checksum, feature contract, alert policy, and monitoring reference. Missing lineage must fail explicitly rather than resemble valid content evidence.

Platform consistency

The CI workflow resolves dependency ranges, while the Docker build pins the scientific stack but resolves serving extras separately. The observed native API used Python 3.12.14 and FastAPI 0.162.7; the built container used Python 3.12.16 and FastAPI 0.165.0.

The locally measured image is Linux ARM64. Cloud deployment automation instead defaults to Linux AMD64, matching the ECS task platform. Lambda exposes a separate architecture parameter. Consequently, the local smoke result and the cloud build are different platform records, not interchangeable binaries.

Learning: lock dependencies and preserve platform-specific image identity with model identity. A successful ARM64 smoke test alone is not an AMD64 test.

CI coverage and required checks

Local validation had the optional checks installed. The current workflow installs only serving/test extras, so the Pandera hard-rule tests can skip on a clean CI environment. CloudFormation linting and controlled model-quality/promotion gates are not part of this workflow. Existing tracking tests primarily use a fake MLflow client; the real local integration was exercised separately in this run.

Improvement: make required extras/checks explicit, fail unexpected skips, add infrastructure validation and a small real local tracking integration check, and retain aggregate validation evidence. Do not upload patient-level data to public CI to achieve this.

Source-version boundary

The numerical experiments and robustness probes describe the research implementation identified in Appendix A. The cloud architecture describes the extended deployment templates and application adapters identified in Appendix C. New cloud functionality does not retroactively change the recorded 145-test result, repair the missing Git revision of that run, or establish that every research-pipeline robustness issue is resolved.

Learnings and recommended next actions

Engineering and model learnings

Learning Evidence and consequence
Verify data content, not directory names. One local copy was incomplete; counts and canonical hashes identified the complete copy.
Successful execution is narrower than complete assurance. All 145 tests passed, while three adversarial control probes exposed missing invariants.
Preserve metric semantics. Hourly decisions, notifications, utility, early recall, and false-alert denominators answer different questions.
A notification budget is not a sensitivity guarantee. B burden remained below budget while early recall and utility fell.
Source shift is both a data and a performance concern. B passed schema but raised persistent input/missingness and settled-label performance alarms.
Match training, serving, and deployment contracts. Native parity passed; S3 URI/hash binding carries explicit model identity into Lambda and Fargate serving.
Separate cloud roles clearly. Fargate runs training and hosted tools in the development profile; Lambda serves scoring. Alternative backends are selected through parameters, not assumed to run simultaneously.
Treat insufficient evidence explicitly. Sparse subgroup windows and absent uncertainty estimates prevent strong fairness or clinical conclusions.
Keep claims and documentation versioned. Earlier design/risk documents predate this execution. New real-data evidence updates those historical execution claims, not all open risks.

Prioritized future work

The following extensions prioritize reproducibility, robustness, and operational maturity. They are future work, not new clinical acceptance thresholds.

Priority / gate Action Proposed owner Objective evidence for closure
P0: before new model promotion Enforce hospital/split binding and semantic compatibility in the research pipeline. Data engineering and MLOps Adversarial regression cases reject unsafe inputs/changes; correct cases retain parity.
P1: release identity Preserve cloud image, model, source, and platform identity in one release manifest. Serving/platform engineering Immutable image identity, expected model checksum, and retained scoring/health results.
P1: release hardening Extend required CI checks and dependency locks across the delivery path. MLOps and platform engineering Workflow/run reference, controlled locks, required extras, and aggregate deployment test evidence.
P1: recovery verification Rehearse coordinated rollback across application and model artifacts. Platform engineering Post-deploy tests and rollback evidence covering compute, model, policy, and monitoring reference.
P1: before performance acceptance Quantify uncertainty and investigate cohort/window failures. Model validation Patient/stay-bootstrap intervals, calibration/PR reporting, reviewed internal utility alarm, and prespecified gates.
P2: monitoring verification Reconcile AWS telemetry, delayed-label joining, schedules, and notifications with offline monitoring. Operations and data engineering Deployed component mapping and end-to-end monitoring/failed-job alert evidence.
Separate authorization Review privacy, licensing, clinical protocol, and independent prospective evaluation. Accountable project/domain reviewers Explicit approvals and new governed evidence; not inferred from this report.

Investigations must not use B outcomes to retune choices and then continue describing B as an independent test. Any changes motivated by these results need a separately governed evaluation design. Do not relax monitoring thresholds merely to make the current alarms disappear.

Limitations and conclusion

The principal limitations are:

  1. One fixed stay-level split, one public source pair, and already inspected external data. Repeating the same experiment is numerical reproduction, not a new independent generalization study.
  2. No patient/stay-bootstrap confidence intervals, prospective validation, causal treatment-effect evidence, or clinical acceptance thresholds.
  3. Missing person identifiers, heavy missingness, administrative measurement effects, first-row-positive records, and post-onset positive labels.
  4. An inferred retrospective onset and conditional lead-time denominator; the nine-hour detected-case median is not a population-wide promise.
  5. Local synthetic API load, short scenarios, same-host networking, and no production availability, security, disaster recovery, or sustained-load assessment.
  6. Offline simulated monitoring, non-evaluated tails, and insufficient subgroup windows. No prospective fairness finding is justified.
  7. Missing Git revision and open release controls despite successful data/split hashing and numerical agreement.
  8. The repository records an unresolved data-redistribution/licence-notice review under R14. This execution did not resolve it or authorize sharing data, model files, or individual trajectories.
  9. The reported latency and test timings are local measurements, not cloud performance guarantees. Environment flags control optional cloud resources; the architecture does not imply every supported mode is enabled.

Project conclusion

The project delivered a reproducible cross-hospital research pipeline, full-cohort model comparison, calibrated scoring, alert-policy evaluation, experiment tracking, retrospective monitoring, and an AWS delivery platform. The recorded run passed 145 tests, processed 40,336 ICU stays, and reproduced the supplied aggregate results. Native batch/API parity and synthetic container operation completed successfully.

The principal model finding is a measurable transportability gap: Hospital B AUROC was 0.7635, normalized utility 0.2340, and early-detection recall 0.4393. The model reduced false-alert burden by 91.5% relative to SIRS, but detected fewer eligible septic stays. Meeting a notification budget therefore cannot substitute for assessing clinical sensitivity.

The principal engineering contribution is the separation of model lifecycle and runtime concerns: Step Functions/Fargate training, MLflow tracking, approval-based publication, checksum-bound Lambda scoring, and explicit telemetry and drift paths. Future work should strengthen split/feature contracts, quantify uncertainty, preserve immutable release lineage, and evaluate prospective performance. Clinical deployment requires a separate validation and authorization process.

Appendix B: recorded execution commands

These excerpts describe the completed run. The existing destinations must not be overwritten. For a new execution, choose a fresh RUN, verify the dataset, and initialize an isolated local MLflow experiment/artifact location as in the training runbook. Use the recorded environment rather than silently resolving newer packages.

PY=.venv/bin/python
DATA=data/physionet-complete-20261114
RUN=artifacts/local-verification-20261126-1412

export MPLBACKEND=Agg OMP_NUM_THREADS=2
export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=2 MKL_NUM_THREADS=2

"$PY" -m unittest discover -s tests -v
"$PY" -m sepsis_warning prepare \
  --data "$DATA" --output "$RUN/prepared/combined.parquet"
"$PY" -m sepsis_warning split \
  --data "$RUN/prepared/combined.parquet" \
  --output "$RUN/prepared/splits.csv" --seed 42
"$PY" -m sepsis_warning validate \
  --data "$RUN/prepared/combined.parquet" \
  --splits "$RUN/prepared/splits.csv" \
  --output "$RUN/data-checks"
"$PY" -m sepsis_warning train \
  --data "$DATA" --output "$RUN/training" \
  --seed 42 --window 6 --budget 0.2 --cooldown 6 \
  --splits-summary "$RUN/prepared/splits.csv.summary.json" \
  --mlflow-uri "sqlite:///$RUN/mlflow.db"
"$PY" -m sepsis_warning monitor-setup \
  --data "$DATA" --model "$RUN/training/model.joblib" \
  --output "$RUN/monitoring/reference" --seed 42
"$PY" -m sepsis_warning monitor-replay \
  --data "$DATA" --model "$RUN/training/model.joblib" \
  --reference "$RUN/monitoring/reference/monitoring_reference.json" \
  --split external_test --output "$RUN/monitoring/external-test"

The internal monitoring replay used --split internal_test and its own new output directory. Baseline, supplementary analysis, synthetic CI, container, and latency logs are retained alongside the main logs in the recorded run directory. The latency invocation used --hours 24 72 336, --concurrency 1 4 8, --requests 50, and --warmup 5.
